summary:
FLARE-X (Space Combustion Research Intelligence) is an interactive scientific research platform designed to help researchers explore NASA's microgravity combustion experiments and identify gaps in the evidence needed to understand fire behavior in future space habitats.

The platform consolidates 22 NASA Physical Sciences Informatics tables, covering 19 investigations and 1,161 experimental tests, into a searchable and comparable research environment. Users can explore experiments, compare their parameters, examine experimental coverage, and evaluate their relevance to mission scenarios through a transparent, adjustable relevance engine. An evidence-grounded AI research assistant helps users retrieve scientific information with supporting references, while automated PDF briefings make findings easier to share.

FLARE-X also highlights an important research gap: among 989 tests reporting both oxygen concentration and pressure, only 66 fall within the challenge-defined Moon-base atmospheric scenario, and all 66 involve gas flames. Furthermore, none of the 140 solid-material tests reports pressure.

By making existing evidence more accessible and exposing what remains unknown, FLARE-X supports more informed research into fire safety for future space exploration. It is a research-support tool, not a fire-prediction or safety-certification system.
details:
FLARE-X: Space Combustion Research Intelligence

FLARE-X is an interactive scientific research intelligence platform designed to explore NASA's microgravity combustion experiments and assess their relevance to future space habitats, particularly lunar missions.

Fire behaves differently in microgravity because the absence of normal buoyancy-driven convection changes how flames develop and how heat and combustion products move. Future space habitats may also operate under atmospheric conditions that differ significantly from Earth's. Although NASA has conducted numerous combustion experiments in space, their results are distributed across different investigations and experimental datasets, making it difficult to compare findings, identify relevant evidence, and understand where important knowledge gaps remain.

FLARE-X addresses this challenge by bringing together and structuring experimental data from 22 original NASA Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI) tables, covering 19 investigations and 1,161 experimental tests. It provides an integrated environment where users can explore investigations, compare experiments, visualize experimental conditions, and evaluate how existing research relates to specific mission scenarios.

The platform includes a Habitat Relevance Engine that allows users to configure mission environments and rank experiments according to their relevance. Its transparent, adjustable scoring methodology considers experimental parameters and mission requirements rather than claiming to predict actual fire behaviour. Interactive visualizations help users identify areas with strong experimental coverage and areas where evidence remains limited.

One of the platform's important findings concerns the challenge-defined Moon-base atmospheric scenario, characterized by oxygen concentrations of at least 30% and pressure of no more than 10.2 psi. Among the 989 experiments reporting both oxygen concentration and pressure, only 66 fall within this scenario, and all 66 are gas-flame experiments. Furthermore, none of the 140 solid-material tests reports pressure. These findings highlight an important limitation in the available experimental evidence and demonstrate the value of identifying not only what research tells us, but also what it does not yet establish.

FLARE-X also incorporates an evidence-grounded AI Research Copilot. Instead of generating unsupported scientific answers, the Copilot retrieves relevant experimental records and platform evidence, provides traceable references, and declines to answer when sufficient supporting evidence is unavailable. The platform also generates PDF research briefings to facilitate the communication and reuse of findings.

The project was developed using Python and FastAPI for the backend, HTML, CSS, and JavaScript for the interactive frontend, and Pandas and NumPy for data processing and analysis. BM25-based information retrieval supports evidence discovery, while an optional locally hosted Ollama language model provides AI-assisted research interaction. ReportLab is used for PDF generation. Git, GitHub, Docker, and automated testing support development, version control, packaging, and deployment.

The creativity of FLARE-X lies in combining scientific data consolidation, mission-oriented relevance assessment, experimental coverage analysis, and evidence-grounded AI in one platform. Rather than presenting NASA datasets as isolated collections of results, it transforms them into an interactive research environment that helps users investigate the relationship between existing experiments and future space mission requirements.

Throughout development, our team considered scientific accuracy, data provenance, experimental comparability, missing information, unit consistency, and the limitations of applying microgravity findings to lunar or Martian environments. We deliberately distinguished measured experimental data from derived values and user-defined scenario assumptions. We also avoided presenting relevance scores as safety predictions or treating microgravity experiments as direct substitutes for partial-gravity experiments.

Our intended impact is to make space-combustion research more accessible, interpretable, and useful for future research and mission planning. By revealing both relevant experimental evidence and areas where further investigation is needed, FLARE-X supports more informed scientific exploration and contributes to the long-term goal of improving fire-safety research for human space exploration.
